Well it’s hard to be anything but agog at a new Robyn Weintraub offering, whose puzzles we have been awaiting with bated breath. And as usual we were given a pretty pristine grid, that even the most die-hard trivia complainers should be happy about, without a hint of a Natick—unless maybe TIA and EDITH, but who can be mad about a call out to the ageless Lily Tomlin? https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=GIaydiPi-zY&pp=0gcJCYsCo7VqN5tD&ra=m And lots of lovely Weintraubian clues like SANTA and GSUIT and TELETHON and GLITTERPEN and IOTA. That said, alas, it was over far too soon for me, suggesting that the insidious tendrils of the Great Easening, like the invasion of the body snatchers, has wormed their way into the puzzles of even our most celebrated enigmatologists, and it’s only a matter of time before all of us, I suppose, will be shuffling along and sending piercing shrieks at anyone daring to create a puzzle that can’t be solved in less time than an unboxing video of an iPhone. That’s ok, it was still worth it to see a master at work and another fun and brilliant grid, thanks Robyn!

DONUT HOLES are mentioned in the column but I still don't get it. How can a hole be a treat? Isn't it just air? Or do you call a donut with a hole in it a "donut hole"?

Polish donuts are pączki, singular: pączek; the word shares its etymology with the adjective "pękaty", meaning round or fat. As I've mentioned here before, Polish donuts never come with a hole. They are shaped like flattened balls, traditionally fried in lard, filled with rose hip jam, and very lightly iced. Historically, Poles gorge on them on Tłusty Czwartek, Fat Thursday, the last Thursday before lent. On that day, many people queue for hours to get their pączki from the most famous bakeries (and I get my pączki from a wonderful, local bakery where there is never a line 🤷🏽).

I think “the Great Easening” is perhaps a bit of a melodramatic moniker. People enjoy crosswords for a variety of reasons, but generally appear (to me) to fall into two camps.

One group loves puzzles for the trivia and therefore enjoys Sam E. for the arcane, reaching-into-the-murky-depths-of-once-heard-names style of puzzle. These puzzles tend to be “harder” because if you don’t know enough proper nouns, you simply cannot complete them.

The other group tends to enjoy crosswords for their wordplay and clever turns of phrase and favors puzzles like Robyn’s, where the trivia takes a backseat to the turns of phrase.

Neither is wrong, but puzzles have increasingly become one way or another (in my estimation.) The two approaches tend to be mutually exclusive, given the limited grid space means any trivia necessarily takes away from any wordplay clues, and vice versa.

Puzzles aren’t getting easier, it’s just that fewer of them rely exclusively on your knowledge of athletes, actors, artists; poets, politicians, philosophers; musicians, magicians, mathematicians; or even news anchors, nautical terms, or other such nonsense.

@Edward

I would disagree with that. There might be a morsel of truth to that; but I think there are lots of ways to jazz up the clues for even the most mundane and non-trivial entries. And even if that was the truth, and there is a trend to studiously avoid most trivia, I would personally call that part of the Great Easening and push against it. Yeah, avoid Naticks for sure and hyper obscure entries; but learning about interesting cultural icons, even newer ones, is not nonsense in my book but one of the joys of solving, both to learn new things, recall fond memories of others (see Edith Ann today) and even share with other commentators. As I’ve said before, it would be a sad puzzle  that had only words and phrases I already know.

And one more observation from a constructor’s point of view. Some themed puzzles have, let’s call it, fewer degrees of freedom in order to make the theme work. Sometimes you have to compromise and allow for a bit more trivia or clunkier fill for a really clever theme or complex theme. For some folks it’s not worth it and for others (including myself) it is. Just something else to take into account.

@Gareth I know we're joking about product placement in crosswords, but there is a reason you're seeing ETSY so much! It has nothing to do with endorsement and everything to do with the letters E, T, S and Y, which are all very common (especially at the end of a word). It's the same reason you'll see STYE so often, and, to a lesser extent, the dreaded TSE-TSE. 

These words are sometimes described as "glue" for puzzles — the often-necessary tradeoff of building crosswords with satisfying entries or a great theme. Few constructors want to reuse words that have appeared hundreds of times, but sometimes you can't make an omelet without a few OREOS :)
